title: Simultaneous Occurrence of HER2 Mutations in EGFR Mutant NSCLC: Case Reports
author: Blerina Resuli; Diego Kauffmann-Guerrero; Jürgen Behr; Amanda Tufman
text:
Abstract
HER2 mutation and amplification have been identified as distinct molecular targets in lung cancer with different therapeutic and prognostic values. The coexistence of HER2 and EGFR mutations is extremely rare, and therefore, no data exist on the best treatment in these cases.
Keywords: Afatinib, Case report, EGFR mutation, HER2 mutations, Non–small cell lung cancer, Osimertinib
Introduction
In the past decade, the identification of oncogenic driver mutations has triggered the development of novel therapeutic approaches, improving clinical outcomes in patients with NSCLC. The treatment paradigm for the management of advanced NSCLC has shifted from a chemotherapy-based approach to molecularly targeted approaches.1 Here, we report two cases of coexistence of EGFR and HER2 mutation treated at our hospital: one with a long-lasting response to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) and the other with a poor response.
Case 1
A 44-year-old patient who had never smoked was diagnosed in May 2018 as having metastatic lung adenocarcinoma with a mass in the right lower lobe and multiple lung and bone metastases.
At baseline, next-generation sequencing Oncomine Focus Assay was positive for EGFR mutation in exon 19 (EGFR L747P) and a comutation in ERBB2 gene (p.K762R). After a first surgical decompression laminectomy of lumbar vertebrae, followed by external beam radiotherapy, the patient received, in June 2018, first-line osimertinib 80 mg once daily. Because of persistent radiologic response, the patient continued osimertinib for 11 months. After progression, cisplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab were administered as second-line treatment for seven months. Pemetrexed and pembrolizumab as maintenance therapy were administered only for two cycles owing to nephrotoxicity. The maintenance treatment was continued only with pembolizumab.
In November 2019, owing to oligoprogressive disease in the brain, stereotactic radiosurgery was administered, and pembrolizumab was continued.
In February 2020, owing to the progression of the disease and the coexpression of the EGFR and the HER2 mutation, the patient received afatinib 40 mg once daily. During the therapy, she experienced grade 1 dermatitis and grade 2 transaminitis.
After progression in February 2021, the liquid biopsy (LB) revealed an EGFR deletion in exon 19 L747P, in addition to the presence of the resistance mutation on exon 20 T790M with the loss of the ERBB2 gene mutation. At that time, we decided to add osimertinib 40 mg once daily and continue afatinib 30 mg once daily.
In November 2021, the disease progressed within the lung and bone. A new LB was performed, and it revealed the original EGFR mutation coupled with the new onset TP53 mutation in exon 7 (M246L) with the loss of the mutation in the ERBB2 gene. At that time, owing to grade 2 renal toxicity, the patient received only osimertinib.
In January 2022, owing to rapid clinical deterioration and the development of a leptomeningeal carcinomatosis, the patient was referred to a palliative care specialist (Fig. 1).
Case 2
The second patient was a 47-year-old man with stage IIIA poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed in December 2021. At that time, he was considered resectable and underwent a video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery left upper lobectomy, lumpectomy, and wedge resection, followed by adjuvant cisplatin and pemetrexed chemotherapy for four cycles. After eight months, disease recurrence developed in both the patient’s lungs. A molecular test performed on the LB revealed the presence of EGFR L858R mutation in exon 21, TP53 duplication (V73RfsX76) in exon 4, and G776delins VC, a typical HER2 exon 20 deletion-insertion. In September 2023, the patient started treatment for metastatic disease with afatinib 40 mg once daily. After progression in December 2023 and a negative LB result, the patient was given pembrolizumab plus pemetrexed-carboplatin and subsequent pembrolizumab plus pemetrexed. The treatment is ongoing, and the patient tolerated the treatment well (Fig. 2).
Discussion
During the past decade, comprehensive molecular assessment has become a standard part of NSCLC management.2 However, not all oncogenic driver alterations have effective target therapies, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic agents.
We described two case reports with coexisting HER2 and EGFR mutation, one showing a response to EGFR TKI and the other with a poorer outcome, probably because of an upfront TP53 mutation.
Early studies described HER2 mutations as mutually exclusive with other oncogenic driver mutations, such as EGFR mutation.3 Nevertheless, a retrospective analysis of real-world data reported that less than 1% of patients with NSCLC had comutations in HER2 and EGFR.4 This study found that in patients with concurrent EGFR mutation and HER2 mutations, the median time on treatment with EGFR TKIs was significantly longer than in those with EGFR mutation without HER2 alterations.4
In accordance with this data, our first patient had a long-lasting response to EGFR TKIs. The co-occurrence of TP53 in the second case was associated with worse response to EGFR TKIs. TP53 concomitant mutations are associated with shorter progression-free survival and overall survival in advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC treated with TKIs, regardless of the type of TKI (first-second versus third generation).
Liu et al.5 reported that osimertinib had antitumor efficacy against multiple HER2 aberrations in NSCLC, either as a single agent or in combination with JQ1, a bromodomain and extraterminal protein inhibitor in a preclinical study using animal models. Because of the homology between HER2 and EGFR, it has been speculated that the covalent binding site for osimertinib may be C805 (analogous Cys797 to EGFR) of human HER2.5
Conclusion
To the best of our knowledge, coexistent HER2 and EGFR mutations in NSCLC are extremely rare and have no specific approved target therapies. These cases provide evidence to help clinicians identify the therapeutic regimen for such patients, and highlight the role of LB as a powerful diagnostic tool in detecting targetable driver events.
